attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, giving his own finding.

semantics.note: Faithful to the statement. The 'should have been disclosed' part is a value judgment that sits inside a factual claim. The contract rightly leaves it unscored and tests only the ownership fact and whether the testimony left it out.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary. It treats an LP interest in a fund that holds OpenAI equity as an 'indirect stake', and 'half the truth' as leaving that out. Fixing the test to the hearing date fits the Senate comparison Marcus drew. It does not rule on any legal duty.

evidence.note: Hearing transcript dated 2023-05-16. It shows the flat 'no equity' answer with no mention of an indirect holding, and the packet says it was cross-checked against the official record.

OpenAI's own disclosure, archived the day after the hearing. It says his only interest was indirect, through a YC fund. As a company disclosure it backs up the ownership fact but is not an independent finding.

News report published 2026-05-13, before the evaluation date. It covers Altman's sworn trial testimony admitting economic exposure through his LP position in the YC fund, and that he left it out of the Senate testimony. This places the interest at the time of the hearing.

reviews.rationale: The transcript shows the flat answer that he had no equity. OpenAI's disclosure the next day and Altman's later sworn admission, as reported, show he had an indirect economic interest through a YC fund at the time and did not mention it. That meets the support condition. The packet contains no counterevidence. The disclosure judgment is Marcus's opinion and is not scored.
